featured.name: Haughton Crater, Devon Island
featured.headline: Polar desert impact crater with ground ice.
featured.description: Haughton is a roughly 20 km wide impact crater on one of the largest uninhabited islands on Earth. It sits in a cold, dry polar desert with permafrost and very little plant cover. Research teams have used it for decades to rehearse Moon and Mars field operations.
shortfalls: Thin vegetation and liquid water in summer
Sun sets for months in winter instead of grazing the horizon

featured.name: Yungay, Atacama Desert
featured.headline: One of the driest places on Earth.
featured.description: The Yungay area of the Atacama receives almost no rain, and its soils hold very little life. Strong sunlight and oxidising salts in the soil echo conditions on the Martian surface. Rover and life-detection instruments are regularly tested here.

featured.name: Wright Valley, McMurdo Dry Valleys
featured.headline: Ice-free polar valley with buried ice and extreme cold.
featured.description: The Dry Valleys are among the coldest and driest ice-free places on Earth. Strong winds remove snow, leaving bare rock, sand and ice-cemented ground. Patterned ground and buried ice here resemble features seen in the Martian mid-latitudes.
shortfalls: Much warmer than the lunar poles

featured.name: Askja caldera
featured.headline: Barren basaltic volcanic field where Apollo crews trained.
featured.description: Askja is a volcanic caldera surrounded by fresh lava and pumice with almost no plant cover. Apollo astronauts trained here in the 1960s to recognise volcanic geology. Basaltic surfaces and lava flows make it a strong compositional match for lunar maria.
shortfalls: Much smaller temperature swings than the Moon

featured.name: Kīlauea summit and Kaʻū Desert
featured.headline: Young basaltic lava fields and lava tubes.
featured.description: The Kaʻū Desert on the flank of Kīlauea is covered in recent basaltic lava and ash, with sparse plants due to volcanic gases and rain shadow. Fresh basalt here is chemically close to lunar mare basalt, and the area is used to test regolith handling and rovers.
matches: Sparse vegetation in the desert zone
shortfalls: Warm and humid compared with any lunar site

featured.name: Mars Desert Research Station
featured.headline: Layered red sedimentary desert used for Mars simulations.
featured.description: The badlands around the station expose layered sedimentary rock coloured by iron oxides, much like the layered terrain in Gale Crater. Crews live in a simulated habitat and run field missions in suits.

featured.name: Cueva de los Verdes lava tube
featured.headline: Kilometres-long lava tube used for cave training.
featured.description: This lava tube runs for several kilometres beneath basaltic lava fields. Lunar and Martian lava tubes could shelter habitats from radiation and temperature swings, and astronaut cave training has used tubes on Lanzarote. Scores here describe the surface only.
shortfalls: Surface score only, the tube interior is not modelled

featured.name: Danakil Depression
featured.headline: Hot, salty, volcanic basin below sea level.
featured.description: The Danakil is one of the hottest places on Earth, with salt flats, acidic hot springs and basaltic volcanoes. Brines and evaporite minerals here help scientists understand salty deposits found in ancient Martian lake basins.
shortfalls: Extremely hot, unlike any Mars site
